modules.title: The Georgian Alphabet
modules.subtitle: 33 letters, one sound each
modules.intro: Mkhedruli has 33 letters and no capitals, though signs often use a taller style of the same letters. Each letter has one sound, so once you know them you can read any word aloud.

lessons.title: Tight or with air?
lessons.note: Five sounds have two versions: tight, with no air (კ პ ტ წ ჭ), and with a puff of air, like English (ქ ფ თ ც ჩ). They make different words: კარი is a door, ქარი the wind.
lessons.subtitle: კ/ქ  პ/ფ  ტ/თ …

modules.title: Essential Vocabulary
modules.subtitle: The words you need first
modules.intro: Ten themes of everyday words, each with an example sentence.

intro.title: Hello means victory
intro.text: გამარჯობა comes from გამარჯვება, victory: you wish someone victory. The reply, გაგიმარჯოს, wishes it back. Morning, evening and night greetings end in მშვიდობისა, "of peace": დილა მშვიდობისა is "morning of peace".

intro.title: Two kinds of thanks
intro.text: მადლობა is everyday thanks. გმადლობთ is polite: the გ- means "you" and the -თ makes it polite. You'll meet this -თ everywhere.

intro.title: Called, not named
intro.text: Georgian says "to me it is called": მე ნინო მქვია. The მ- inside the verb is "me". To ask: რა გქვია? with გ- for "you".

intro.title: From where
intro.text: საიდან means "from where": სად (where) + -იდან (from). -იდან replaces a final -ი or -ა: თბილისიდან, from Tbilisi. Words in -ო add just -დან: კინოდან, from the cinema.

intro.title: Counting to ten
intro.text: Georgian numbers are short and regular. After a number the noun stays singular: ორი ჩაი, "two tea". No plural to worry about.

intro.title: Ten and more
intro.text: The teens are built from ten and the number: თ (from ათი, ten) + ოთხ (four) + მეტი (more) makes თოთხმეტი, fourteen. Look for the pattern in each one.

intro.title: Counting in twenties
intro.text: Above twenty Georgian counts in twenties: ორმოცი is "two twenties". The next lesson shows how to build every number from these.

lessons.title: How numbers are built

notes.title: Eleven to nineteen: ten and more
notes.text: Every teen is თ + the number + მეტი, "more": თ-ოთხ-მეტი is "ten, four more", fourteen. Before ს, შ and ც the თ melts into the sound: ცამეტი (13), ჩვიდმეტი (17), ცხრამეტი (19). In 18, -რვ- turns to -ვრ-: თვრამეტი.

table.en: 13: თ + სამ + მეტი, თს melts into ც
17: თ + შვიდ + მეტი, თშ melts into ჩ
18: თ + რვა + მეტი, რვ turns to ვრ
19: თ + ცხრა + მეტი, თც melts into ც

notes.title: Counting in twenties
notes.text: From twenty up, Georgian counts in twenties, a little like French quatre-vingts (four twenties, 80). ორმოცი is "two twenties", სამოცი "three twenties", ოთხმოცი "four twenties".

notes.title: Twenty and…
notes.text: To go past a twenty, drop its last ი, add და ("and"), then a number from 1 to 19. So 21 is "twenty and one", 30 is "twenty and ten" and 31 is "twenty and eleven".

notes.title: A number and a noun
notes.text: After a number the noun stays singular: ორი ყავა is "two coffee". When the noun takes an ending, the number drops its ი: შვიდ საათზე, "at seven o'clock".

lessons.subtitle: Eleven to nineteen: ten and more

intro.title: Food words
intro.text: Most nouns end in -ი in their plain form: პური, ყველი. When the word does a job in the sentence, the -ი gives way to another ending: ყველს ვჭამ, I eat cheese.

intro.title: Georgian kitchen
intro.text: ხაჭაპური and ხინკალი are names you'll see on every menu. Words for things you eat often come in the singular: ხილი is fruit, ბოსტნეული vegetables.

intro.title: Getting around
intro.text: Most transport words are international: ავტობუსი, მეტრო, ტაქსი. -ით means "by": მანქანით, by car. Words ending in -ო add -თი: მეტროთი, by metro.

intro.title: Travelling far
intro.text: Long words are often built from parts: თვითმფრინავი is "self-flying". აეროპორტი and სადგური take -ში for "to": აეროპორტში, to the airport.

intro.title: Directions
intro.text: მარჯვნივ (to the right) and მარცხნივ (to the left) differ in the middle: -ჯვ- for right, -ცხ- for left. The polite "turn" is მოუხვიეთ: you'll say it in every taxi.

intro.title: Near and far
intro.text: ახლოს and შორს are said with არის, is: ახლოს არის, it's near. Put the place first: ბაზარი ახლოს არის?

intro.title: Shops and prices
intro.text: რა ღირს? literally "what is it worth?": the everyday "how much?". ღია and დაკეტილი, open and closed, are on every shop door.

intro.title: Paying
intro.text: ლარი is the money; თეთრი is the small change, 100 tetri to a lari. თეთრი also means "white". By card is ბარათით: ბარათი + -ით, "with the card".

intro.title: Mother and father
intro.text: Careful: დედა is mother and მამა is father, the opposite of what you might expect. შვილი is someone's child, ბავშვი a child in general.

intro.title: The whole family
intro.text: და means both "sister" and "and": the sentence makes it clear. ჩემი, my, never changes: ჩემი ძმა, my brother; ჩემი და, my sister.

intro.title: At home
intro.text: Places take -ში for "in": სახლში, at home; ოთახში, in the room. Things on top take -ზე: მაგიდაზე, on the table.

intro.title: Things around you
intro.text: To say a thing is somewhere, add -ა (short for არის, is) to the place: წიგნი მაგიდაზეა, the book is on the table.

intro.title: Today and tomorrow
intro.text: Time words need no little words before them: დღეს, today; ხვალ, tomorrow. დილით and საღამოს are "in the morning" and "in the evening".

intro.title: Days of the week
intro.text: From Monday to Thursday the days count from Saturday: ორშაბათი is "two after Saturday". კვირა is both Sunday and week.

modules.title: Everyday Georgian
modules.subtitle: Phrases for real situations
modules.intro: Whole phrases you can use straight away: in cafés, shops, taxis and at the doctor's.

intro.title: Asking politely
intro.text: In cafés Georgians add თუ შეიძლება, "if it's possible", after what they ask for: მენიუ, თუ შეიძლება. It's the everyday please.

intro.title: At the shop
intro.text: To buy, say the amount, then the thing: ერთი კილო ვაშლი. To check the price: რა ღირს ეს? Bargaining is normal at a bazaar.

intro.title: In a taxi
intro.text: Drivers say თქვენ to you, the polite you, with -თ on the verb: სად მიდიხართ? Answer with the place and -ში: აეროპორტში.

intro.title: Asking the way
intro.text: Commands to strangers end in -თ: წადით, go; მოუხვიეთ, turn. If you don't follow, ვერ გავიგე: "I couldn't catch it".

intro.title: Meeting neighbours
intro.text: With neighbours you don't know yet, use the polite forms: როგორ ხართ? With friends: როგორ ხარ?

intro.title: Saying what hurts
intro.text: Georgian says "to me hurts": თავი მტკივა, my head hurts. The body part is the subject.

intro.title: At work
intro.text: ვმუშაობ is "I work": ვ- for I. Where you work takes -ში: ოფისში ვმუშაობ.

intro.title: Small talk
intro.text: Weather is said with one word: ცხელა, it's hot; ცივა, it's cold. რა + the short -ა (is) makes an exclamation: რა ამინდია! What weather!

modules.title: Grammar
modules.subtitle: How sentences fit together
modules.intro: Small, friendly steps into Georgian grammar: just what you need to build your own sentences.

notes.title: Personal pronouns
notes.text: Georgian has six. There is no he or she: ის means he, she and it. It also means "that"; "this" is ეს.

exercises.explanation: ჩვენ is we; თქვენ is you (plural or polite).
Georgian doesn't mark he or she.

exercises.prompt: Talking politely to an older stranger, "you" is…
exercises.explanation: თქვენ is the polite you, even for one person.
ვართ is "we are", so the pronoun is ჩვენ.

notes.title: I am, you are
notes.text: The verb "to be" changes with the person. It usually comes at the end of the sentence.

notes.title: The short -ა
notes.text: არის is often shortened to -ა at the end of the word before it.

exercises.explanation: -ა at the end is short for არის.

notes.title: The present tense
notes.text: The start and end of a verb show who is doing it: ვ- for I and we, -ს for he or she, -თ for plural, -ენ for they, nothing for you. The pronoun is often left out: ვწერ alone is "I write".

notes.title: Word order
notes.text: The verb usually comes last: მე ქართულს ვსწავლობ, "I Georgian learn". Other orders are fine too.

exercises.prompt: In ის წერს, which part means "he / she"?

lessons.title: Want, love, have

notes.title: Verbs that work the other way
notes.text: Some everyday verbs put "me" inside the verb with მ-, and "you" with გ-. The thing you want or have stays in its plain form.

notes.title: Regular verbs
notes.text: Others work like ვწერ.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "I want coffee"?

lessons.subtitle: Verbs that work the other way

notes.title: Question words
notes.text: The question word usually comes just before the verb.

notes.title: Yes or no
notes.text: Keep the sentence as it is and change only the melody: the voice goes up near the end. Copy it from the audio.

exercises.prompt: How do you turn ყავა გინდა into a question?
options: Raise your voice at the end
exercises.explanation: Yes/no questions are the same words, asked.

notes.title: Not, can't, don't
notes.text: Georgian has three "nots", all right before the verb: არ, not; ვერ, can't (ვერ გავიგე, I couldn't catch it); ნუ, don't, when asking someone (ნუ ღელავ, don't worry). არა on its own is "no".

exercises.explanation: ნუ asks someone not to do something.

options: At the end of the sentence

notes.title: Cases
notes.text: A Georgian noun changes its ending to show its job in the sentence. Five to start with:

exercises.explanation: With verbs like this, the thing takes -ს.
-ით: with. შაქარი loses its second ა: შაქრით.

notes.title: Endings for places
notes.text: Where English puts a little word before, Georgian adds an ending.

exercises.translation: The book is on the table.

notes.title: Three patterns for every day
notes.text: მჭირდება and მომწონს work like მინდა, with მ- for "me". შეიძლება is "it is possible": on its own it asks "may I?".

notes.title: Two ways to have
notes.text: Georgian has two verbs for "have": მაქვს for things, მყავს for people and animals. Both put "me" inside the verb with მ-, like მინდა, and "you" with გ-.

exercises.explanation: A phone is a thing: მაქვს.
გ- for you, and a brother is a person.

notes.title: Plurals with -ები
notes.text: Most nouns drop their final -ი and add -ები: სახლი, სახლები. Nouns ending in a vowel keep it: დედა, დედები. A few lose a vowel inside, as in მეგობრები.

notes.title: Not after numbers
notes.text: After a number the noun stays singular: სამი წიგნი, "three book". The plural is only for "books" with no number.

notes.title: Plural things, singular verb
notes.text: Things in the plural often take "is", not "are": სახლები დიდია, the houses are big. For people the verb is plural: მეგობრები ცხოვრობენ.

exercises.explanation: ცხოვრობენ is "they live", so the plural: მეგობრები.

notes.title: The polite -თ
notes.text: Georgian has a polite "you": თქვენ, which is also "you" for several people. The verb gets -თ at the end: გაქვს becomes გაქვთ, იცი becomes იცით. Use it with strangers, in shops, with older people and officials.

notes.title: Polite requests
notes.text: Requests end in -თ too, and თუ შეიძლება makes them softer still: აქ გამიჩერეთ, თუ შეიძლება.

exercises.translation: Do you speak English? (to a stranger)

exercises.prompt: To a taxi driver, "stop here" is…
exercises.explanation: -თ: polite. გამიჩერე is for a friend.

notes.title: Things you did
notes.text: The past has its own forms: learn these six as words first. Each has ვ- for "I", at the start or after a little prefix: წა-ვ-ედი, და-ვ-ლიე.

notes.title: The object changes
notes.text: In the present the thing you eat takes -ს: ხინკალს ვჭამ. In the past it goes back to its plain form: ხინკალი ვჭამე.

exercises.translation: Yesterday I was at the market.

exercises.explanation: In the past the object is in its plain form.

modules.title: Conversation
modules.subtitle: Put it all together
modules.intro: Short conversations: read them, choose your replies and build the sentences yourself.

intro.title: Your first conversation
intro.text: Choose what you would say. The waiter is polite (რა გნებავთ? what would you like?); you answer with თუ შეიძლება. Tap any word to see why it looks that way.

lines.speaker: Giorgi
lines.ka: გამარჯობა! მე გიორგი ვარ. რა გქვია?
lines.lat: gamarjoba! me giorgi var. ra gkvia?
lines.en: Hi! I'm Giorgi. What's your name?

lines.speaker: Giorgi
lines.en: Nice to meet you, Ana! Where are you from?

lines.speaker: Giorgi
lines.en: I'm from Tbilisi. Do you know Georgian?

lines.speaker: You
lines.en: I know a little. I'm learning.

intro.title: Introducing yourself
intro.text: Giorgi is your age, so you both say შენ and use friendly forms: რა გქვია? not რა გქვიათ?

lines.speaker: You
lines.en: Hello! How much is this cheese?

intro.title: At the market
intro.text: Prices are numbers + ლარი, with ლარი singular: თხუთმეტი ლარი. Haggling is part of it: ეს ძალიან ძვირია.

intro.title: Taking a taxi
intro.text: To the airport is აეროპორტში: -ში means "into" as well as "in". Agree the price before you set off.

lines.speaker: You
lines.en: Excuse me, where is the metro?

lines.speaker: Passer-by
lines.en: Go straight ahead, then turn left.

lines.speaker: Passer-by
lines.ka: პირდაპირ, მერე მარცხნივ. შორს არ არის.
lines.lat: p'irdap'ir, mere martskhniv. shors ar aris.
lines.en: Straight on, then left. It's not far.

intro.title: Asking the way
intro.text: Listen for მარჯვნივ, მარცხნივ, პირდაპირ. If it's too fast: გაიმეორეთ, თუ შეიძლება.

lines.speaker: Nino
lines.en: Shall we eat khinkali in the evening?

intro.title: Making plans
intro.text: Friends use the informal forms. ვჭამოთ is "let's eat": the -თ here means "we".
